It is wrong to think of either of the van der Waals forces as "bonds"; they are more like interactions. I like to think of all the intermolecular forces as a rating system. Some molecules can hydrogen bond, some have dipoles, and some have van der Waals forces.

That being said, van der Waals forces arise when a molecule does not have any electrostatic activity. Molecules do not like to touch each other, so van der Waals forces ensure that they do not.

I am not sure what you mean by polar bond, as it really isn't an intermolecular force. It is just a way to categorize a bond. For example, a bond between hydrogen and oxygen is a polar bond because the oxygen is very electronegative and pulls electron density away from hydrogen. A bond between carbon and hydrogen is not a polar bond because there isn't really any major difference in electronegativity to have a considerable effect. That being said, if you take two methyl groups and put them around each other, they will still interact when close enough (van der Waals) because there *is* electric activity, just not enough to make the bond polar.

I hope that helps.

That's what I was trying to convey by describing how I viewed the intermolecular forces as a rating system. You "start" with van der Waals forces and progress to various types of intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds, dipole interactions, etc.).

Someone suggested purchasing a book on organic chemistry that serves as a second language, and this is good advice. This book saved me during my first organic chemistry course.

The author emphasizes that "you will excel in organic chemistry if you understand the mechanisms," and he is correct.

The beginning (at least for me) of the second organic chemistry course focuses on carbocation stability (Diels-Alder reactions, 1,2 and 1,4 products for conjugated alkenes, etc.). It's challenging to arrive at the answers through memorization alone.

Each problem will become easier as you recognize similarities between reactions. Understanding mechanisms can be difficult at first, but over time you will appreciate the genuine beauty of organic chemistry.

Additionally, if you prefer math-based classes, I hope you have taken or are planning to take a course in analytical chemistry. It's quite mathematical and is one of my favorite branches of chemistry.

The extraction of caffeine from chocolate products was based on the procedure described by researchers. A clean-up step was added before injection into the chromatograph. Samples of chocolate bars (0.60 g) and chocolate powders (1.0 g) were weighed into test tubes equipped with Teflon-lined screw caps. The fat was extracted by shaking twice with 30 ml portions of petroleum ether and centrifuging at 470.0 g for 10 min. The residual solvent was evaporated by placing the test tubes in a warm water bath. To the residue, water (30 ml) and saturated basic acetate solution (5 ml) were added, followed by centrifugation at 1057.5 g for 5 min. Sodium bicarbonate was added to the supernatant, and the centrifugation was repeated. To the supernatant, 0.1 M hydrochloric acid was added. The solution was then diluted to volume with water into a 100 ml volumetric flask, mixed, and injected into a liquid chromatograph.
